1:
Whether the opening sentence is a definition at all is the first question. Calvin says whoever made this the beginning of the eleventh chapter unwisely disjointed the context, since the apostle was proving what he had already said, that there is need of patience, and Griesbach's division three verses earlier is what the subject requires; those are greatly mistaken who think an exact definition is given here, for the apostle selects only the part of faith suitable to his purpose, that patience is ever connected with it. Ellicott reports the same debate, whether what follows defines what faith is or describes what faith does, and answers that it is no complete definition, but that the things hoped for are not mere figments of the imagination since their basis is the word of God; whether the sentence be called definition or description is then of little consequence. Barnes sets the chapter in its argument: the readers were in the midst of trials and in danger of relapsing into Judaism, faith was the indispensable means of securing them, and since they were Hebrews the apostle appeals to their own history. Robertson calls what follows a chapter of great eloquence and passion, a recital of the heroes of faith whose example should spur them to like loyalty.

On the first term they converge from different directions. Clarke renders it subsistence, that which becomes a foundation for another thing to stand on. Ellicott traces it through the epistle, the essence standing under the qualities possessed and then the steadfastness of a later chapter, and observes that the Authorised version here deserted the earlier English translations, most of which had sure confidence or ground, to follow the Rhemish rendering of the Latin; that sense is not very clear, and the symmetry of the verse almost compels a word denoting an act of the mind. Robertson traces the word from Aristotle on, notes its philosophical use earlier in the epistle, and finds it common in the papyri as the basis or guarantee of business transactions. Henry takes it experientially: the persuasion is so strong that it gives the soul a kind of possession and present fruition, a subsistence by the first-fruits and foretastes. Calvin presses the paradox in it: what we hope for is not what we have in hand, so faith regards not present things but such as are waited for, and the contradiction is not without its force and beauty.

The second term Clarke explains as the conviction produced by the demonstration of a problem, after which no doubt can remain because we see the thing cannot be otherwise; he compares the axioms of geometry and the theorem on the hypotenuse. Henry says it demonstrates to the eye of the mind. Wesley makes a careful distinction between the two halves: things hoped for are not so extensive as things not seen, the former being only future and joyful to us while the latter may be future, past or present.

On the elders, age is not the point. Calvin prefers Macknight and Stuart's rendering, ancients, since the usual word refers to age but ancients to time; and he explains why the Jews needed the correction, a foolish admiration of the fathers having so prevailed that it hindered surrender to Christ. Gill takes them as those who lived in ancient times, some before the flood, others in civil or ecclesiastical office; Robertson denies the technical sense of officers and compares the tradition of the elders. Barnes and Ellicott both render the verb passively, that witness was borne to them. Wesley calls the chapter a kind of summary of the Old Testament and observes that God gave testimony not only of them but to them. Clarke marks what is missing: not one word concerning Adam and his wife, though Abraham and Sarah are named, God having covered their state with an impenetrable veil.
3:
Chrysostom explains why the argument turns to examples. Faith needs a generous and vigorous soul, rising above all things of sense and beyond the weakness of human reasonings, since no one becomes a believer except by raising himself above the common customs of the world. The souls of the Hebrews were weakened; they had begun from faith but from sufferings had become faint-hearted, and so the writer encourages them first from their former days, then from the Scripture that the just shall live by faith, then from argument, and now from their forefathers.

Why creation is the first instance is variously explained. Barnes says it is selected because it is the first thing narrated in the Bible calling for faith; no particular instance is pointed to, since none is recorded, but it illustrates the faith every man may observe in himself. Our knowledge here is a mere matter of credence given the divine testimony: we could not reason it out and demonstrate it, and no profane history goes back so far. Ellicott notes that the first place is not given to the elders, because the writer's object is the achievements of faith, with which the Scripture record is filled; even where there is no history of men, faith is required of us, which the first words of Scripture teach. Robertson observes that every example as far as Rahab is formally introduced by the same instrumental phrase, after which only a summary is given, and that the author appeals to our knowledge of the world these heroes lived in; recent books by great scientists, he adds, confirm that a Supreme Mind is behind and before the universe, and science can only stand still in God's presence and believe like a little child.

What was framed they take variously. Clarke insists the word cannot refer to age or any measurement of time, since the writer speaks of things seen, so it must mean the material fabric of the universe; being plural it may take in not only the earth and visible heavens but the whole planetary system. Ellicott renders it literally that the ages have been prepared, repeating a remarkable expression from the first chapter, the idea being the complete preparation of all that successive periods of time contain. Calvin reports that Beza and others render the plural as a singular, citing Stuart that the singular is not used for the universe while the plural expresses the parts of which the world is composed, though our own word world comprehends the whole; Beza, he adds, renders the verb compacted. Robertson parses it as a perfect passive of a verb meaning to mend or equip. Gill enumerates the celestial world with its angels, the starry with sun and stars, the terrestrial with men and beasts, and the watery with all in the sea; he mentions the rabbinic reckoning of three hundred and ten worlds, and sometimes eighteen thousand, but adds that Philo rightly charged such notions with ignorance and folly. Wesley sums it as heaven and earth and all in them, visible and invisible, formed and finished by the sole command of God without instrument or preceding matter, and adds that as creation is the foundation and specimen of the whole divine economy, so faith in creation is the foundation of all faith.

Clarke argues that the things were not made out of pre-existent matter, for if they were, that matter, however modified, must appear in the thing compounded of it, and then it could not be said that what is seen was not made of what appears; the same words show that the present fabric was not reformed from an anterior one. Wesley allows a chaos but denies it independence: the things seen were made out of the dark, unapparent chaos, and this chaos was itself created by the divine power, having before that no existence in nature.
4:
Gill and Henry pause first over an omission. Gill asks why Adam and Eve are not mentioned, and answers that it is not because they were unbelievers but either because of the ruin of mankind by them, or because the apostle speaks only of those who received eminent testimony. Henry says the church has generally by a pious charity taken it for granted that God gave them repentance and faith in the promised seed and taught them the mystery of sacrificing, but that God has left the matter under doubt as a warning to all entrusted with great talents, since he would not enroll our first parents in this blessed calendar. The list begins instead with Abel, the first martyr for religion, who lived by faith and died for it.

Why his offering was preferred divides them sharply. Calvin allows only one reason: it was preferable for no other than that it was sanctified by faith, and he settles the comparative on quality rather than quantity, so the rendering should be a better sacrifice and not a fuller one. Robertson says flatly that why Abel's sacrifice was better, apart from his faith, is not shown. Ellicott argues the same from the text, since Genesis designates both offerings by the same name in Hebrew and in Greek, so that apart from the opening words nothing here explains the superiority; he allows that one who believes sacrifice was of divine institution may hold it probable that Abel's obedience showed in his manner of approach. Barnes reaches the same conclusion by another road: an offering of the ground's fruits cannot have been displeasing, since the law afterwards commanded it, and each brother naturally brought what he had raised and thought most valuable, so that had the temper of mind been the same in both, each offering would have been accepted.

Against them stand those who find something in the offering itself. Clarke takes the comparative literally as more sacrifice, meaning Abel made more than one offering, which is why the testimony concerns his gifts in the plural: Cain the husbandman brought a eucharistic offering of the ground's fruits, acknowledging the being and providence of God, while Abel the shepherd brought that and also of his flock as a sin-offering, acknowledging his own sinfulness; Cain, not apprehensive of the demerit of sin, contented himself with the thank-offering, which God could not consistently with his holiness receive, there being no sin-offering with it. Wesley reads it the same way in fewer words, the firstlings implying a confession of what his own sins deserved and a desire of sharing in the great atonement, while Cain's offering testified a bare acknowledgment of God the Creator. Gill finds the superiority in matter and manner both: the one offered heartily and the other in show, and Abel looked through his sacrifice to Christ's, his lamb a type of the Lamb of God, a firstling figuring the firstborn of every creature, the fattest of the flock expressing Christ's excellency. Henry calls it a more full and perfect sacrifice and locates the difference in the persons and the principles, Abel acting under the power of faith and Cain from the force of education or natural conscience.

On the testimony, Robertson parses the personal construction by which Abel himself was witnessed to as righteous. Ellicott takes the witness to be borne by God in accepting the offering, shown by some visible sign, such acceptance implying Abel's righteousness and so testifying to his faith. Wesley guesses the sign was fire from heaven consuming the sacrifice, a token that justice seized the victim instead of the sinner. On the last clause Clarke says that by this faith, exercised in reference to an atonement, Abel still preaches to mankind the necessity of one; Wesley, that a sinner is accepted only through faith in the great sacrifice; Robertson, that he speaks still through his faith.
5:
Gill defines the translation by what it was not: no spiritual translation from darkness into the kingdom of Christ; no rapture from one part of the earth to another, as Philip was caught away after the eunuch's baptism; no temporary catching up, as Paul was caught to the third heaven; but a removal from earth to heaven, soul and body, there to continue as Elijah did, by a change from mortality to immortality which is a pledge of the resurrection. Clarke keeps to the plain point that the apostle is explaining the Genesis phrase, so that we learn Enoch did not die and God took him to blessedness without obliging him to pass through death. Ellicott notes the words are an exact quotation from the Greek version, the verb denoting merely change of place, but that nothing equals the simplicity of the Hebrew, he was not, for God took him. Robertson observes that our word metathesis comes from that verb, and marks the imperfect as he was still not found. Wesley adds that men perhaps sought him as they did Elijah.

Calvin asks the question the others pass over, why God removed him in so unusual a manner, and answers from the times. Impiety prevailed everywhere; had Enoch died as other men, no one would have supposed him preserved from the contagion by providence, but taken away without dying, the hand of God from heaven was openly manifested, removing him as from the fire.

Ellicott renders the testimony as he hath had witness borne to him that he hath been well pleasing to God, and shows how the argument fastens to the text: the Greek version renders walked with God as was well pleasing to God, and that rendering is what is quoted, so Scripture withholds the record of the translation until it has first borne this witness. Robertson takes the perfect to mean the record stands still. Barnes concedes that Genesis makes no mention of faith, attributing it as in Abel's case either to the nature of piety or to direct revelation; but he finds it implied in walking with God, and perhaps in what Jude reports of Enoch's prophecy. Wesley locates the testimony in Enoch's own conscience.

The following verse is the proof of what precedes. Calvin says the reason is given in the clause subjoined, that no one comes to God except he believes that God is and is a rewarder of those who seek him; if access is opened by faith alone, all who lack it are objects of God's displeasure, and faith is our teacher as to the true worship of God. Ellicott makes the connection backwards, so the statement that Enoch pleased God asserts faith in him, and no one can be a habitual worshipper whose faith does not grasp these two truths; he renders the second as becometh a recompenser, the future recompense present to the eye of faith. Barnes generalises beyond religion: no child pleases a father, no husband a wife, where confidence is lacking. Robertson calls it a moral necessity holding in business too, with banks for instance, and says the existence of God is a matter of intelligent faith. Clarke spells out what the worshipper must hold, a Being infinite, eternal and self-existent, the cause of all other being, and not indifferent about his own worship. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the clause as an invitation to the true faith and turns it toward the will: when will a man resolve to serve God unless he believes he is a giver of reward, or a young woman choose a virgin life if she believes not that for chastity there is an unfading crown? Faith, he says, is an eye that enlightens the conscience. Gill guards the negative, that without faith no duty is acceptable, such works being without Christ and having neither right principles nor right ends.
7:
Barnes finds this the least difficult case yet, since everything Noah did about the threatened deluge rested on simple belief of what God said. It was not that the course of events tended that way, nor that such a thing had happened before, nor that the belief was common; God had simply informed him, and the admonition came a hundred and twenty years before the flood, long before any natural sign could appear. Calvin turns the same facts into a portrait of magnanimity: while the whole world promised itself impunity and indulged unrestrainedly in sinful pleasures, Noah alone regarded a vengeance long deferred, wearied himself a hundred and twenty years in building, stood unshaken amid the scoffs of the ungodly, and felt sure of life as it were in the grave. He also marks a turn in the argument: the writer has hitherto spoken of the fathers of the first age, whereas the emergence of Noah and his family from the deluge was a kind of regeneration, so that in every age men have been approved by God only by faith. Chrysostom notes what distinguishes this instance from the last: Enoch's example was of faith only, Noah's of unbelief also, and this is consolation and exhortation together, when not only are believers approved but unbelievers suffer the opposite. He adds that the Son of God, speaking of his own coming, recalled the days when they married and were given in marriage, so the writer brings back an appropriate image.

On the warning the interest is lexical. Gill renders it as having received an oracle from God, admonishing Noah how to make an ark, as Moses was afterwards how to make a tabernacle. Clarke says that since Genesis tells us God did warn him, we see here the verb's real import elsewhere in the New Testament, to utter oracles or give divine warning. Robertson parses it as a first aorist passive of the old word for divine communications. Chrysostom asks why the term for a divine communication is used at all, notes that elsewhere a thing is said to be communicated by the Spirit, and infers that the Spirit reveals as God reveals, so that the equal dignity of the Spirit may be seen; the things not seen he identifies simply as the rain.

What the fear was divides them. Clarke takes it as religious reverence toward God, mentioned to show that Noah acted not from fear of losing his life but from the fear of God, so that fear is here properly attributed to faith. Ellicott reports that some prefer the marginal rendering, being wary or taking forethought, which suits the word's proper meaning, but judges it likelier that the writer means the devout godly fear the cognates regularly carry; Noah's obedience evidenced at once that fear and the faith which gave present reality to things not yet seen. Robertson traces the verb to a compound meaning to take hold carefully, hence to act circumspectly, and notes that it occurs here only in the New Testament.

Ellicott observes that the connecting words are slightly ambiguous, relating either to the ark or to the faith, and prefers the faith: it was Noah's faith, shown in the building, that exposed the unbelief of a world which would not listen, and our Lord uses condemn in the same sense of the men of Nineveh. Clarke agrees and quotes Dodd, that a good man's virtues condemn those who will not imitate them: he credited God and they did not, he walked as commanded and they did not, he admonished them and they regarded it not. Wesley calls the ark an open testimony by which he condemned a world that neither believed nor feared. Robertson sets the title of heir beside the description of Noah elsewhere as a preacher of righteousness, and adds that he believed his own message.
8:
Calvin explains why Abraham dominates the chapter: he is the chief father of God's church, in whose name the Jews gloried as though being his holy race set them apart, whereas Abraham had no excellency that did not proceed from faith. Barnes finds the case stronger than Noah's, since Genesis says he believed in the Lord and it was counted for righteousness. Clarke calls the obedience the fullest proof of the faith, and the faith implicit, since Abraham went out with no prospect of good but what faith led him to expect. Robertson calls him a graphic example who did not know where the land was. Ellicott prefers the older versions, which bring in obeyed after called, and corrects a misreading: the promise of the land came after he obeyed, not at the call. Gill takes the call as an emblem of the calling of God's people out from the world. Henry turns it on the reader: if heirs of Abraham's faith we shall go forth not knowing what may befall.

The sojourning is a second and harder trial. Calvin asks where the inheritance was, since having entered the land he was hardly received as a stranger, and might have thought God had deceived him; worse still, a famine soon drove him to Gerar. Clarke observes that he acquired no right in Canaan but a burying place, his faith showing him the land was only a pledge of a better country. Barnes says he owned nothing in fee-simple beyond that grave. Ellicott paraphrases the last clause: Abraham made his home there once for all, expecting no change all his life, and made it in tents, movable and shifting abodes. Wesley adds that Isaac had the inheritance not from Abraham, nor Jacob from Isaac, but all from God.

On the city Barnes rejects the view of Grotius that Jerusalem is meant, since no such promise was made to Abraham and the reading falls below the drift of the passage. Ellicott renders it the city which hath the foundations, and says the promise as the patriarchs grasped it was never bounded by the gift of Canaan. Clarke says Abraham knew earth could afford no permanent residence for an immortal mind, and lost sight of earth to keep heaven in view; the closing titles he distinguishes as the architect who plans and the owner of what is built. Calvin says heaven is called a city for its perpetuity; Robertson marks the imperfect as patient waiting in spite of disappointment; Wesley, that a tent has no foundations; Gill, that the city is the new Jerusalem and the glory of the saints.

Whether Sarah or Abraham is the subject is disputed. Gill reports that some take it of Abraham's faith, rendering the clause because he judged him faithful, the apostle speaking of Abraham both before and after. Calvin holds the example was adduced so that women might know the truth belongs to them, Sarah being the mother of all the faithful; and he grants that her faith is commended who laughed at the word as at a fable, conceding it was blended with unbelief. Barnes says the emphatic pronoun marks something remarkable, her incredulity having been overcome. Clarke observes that her age justified the ridicule while she took the message for no divine one, but that once she knew, she doubted no more. Ellicott allows that the emphasis may point to the unbelief, or mean only that Sarah too had her part. Cyril of Jerusalem sums it: Abraham was justified not only by works but also by faith, and though he did many things well he was never called the friend of God until he believed. On the multitude that followed, Clarke calls Isaac's birth entirely supernatural and its descendants a supernatural people; Barnes marks that a nation sprang from one man; Robertson renders the last phrase along the lip of the sea.
13:
Ellicott and Robertson both notice the change of formula. Seven verses have begun with the emphatic by faith; this one does not, and Ellicott insists the original order must stand, so the sense is not that by faith these died but that in accordance with faith all these died. Robertson calls it a break in the routine, made for variety or, as Moffatt suggests, to present faith as the sphere and standard of their characters. Barnes restricts the phrase to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Sarah, since the promises were not entrusted to Abel and Noah, and including them would force in Enoch, who did not die at all; Calvin limits it the same way. Robertson raises the one difficulty, that the writer elsewhere has Abraham obtain the promise, and answers that he received the promise of the Messiah without living to see him come. Barnes presses the point into the phrase: it means not that they died in the exercise of religion, but without possessing what their faith was set on.

Clarke defines the two words, strangers being persons out of their own country, pilgrims sojourners for a time who never mean to be naturalised; and he asks how many profess to be pilgrims here below while their conduct says otherwise. Calvin finds a comparison enhancing their faith: having only tasted the promises they were satisfied with their sweetness and despised all the world, never forgetting that taste in life or death. Wesley says that in death faith acts most vigorously. Chrysostom goes furthest: the first virtue, indeed the whole of virtue, is to be a stranger to this world, hanging loose from things here as from things strange to us. He points to those of whom the chapter later says that they wandered in sheepskins, of whom the world was not worthy; they called themselves strangers, but Paul went further, saying he was dead to the world and the world dead to him.

The confession then proves the point. Barnes says we should think the same of any strange people among us who lived in tents, often changed residence, bought no land except to bury their dead and never spoke of settling: we should conclude they sought a home and had not found it. Clarke defines a country as that in which a man has constitutional rights, which no sojourner has, and adds that no intelligent Jew could think Canaan all the rest God promised. Ellicott renders the clause as making plain that they seek a fatherland, citing Abraham at Machpelah and Jacob before Pharaoh.

What follows Calvin treats as answering an objection, that they were strangers only because they had left their country: they did not think of Mesopotamia, for had they wished to return they might have, but they willingly banished themselves and disowned it. Barnes says the journey was neither so long nor so perilous that they could not have retraced it, which shows their remaining was voluntary. Robertson parses the second-class condition with imperfects in both halves, so that had they continued mindful they would have kept the opportunity, and remarks that continual hankering would have found a way, as the Israelites hankered after Egypt. Clarke says they held their right to the promises to depend on an utter renunciation of Chaldea, which is why Abraham made his steward swear not to carry Isaac back. On the last verse Calvin takes the title God gave himself at the bush as a singular honour, since when the fathers aspired to a celestial country God counted them citizens, whence there is no place among God's children except we renounce the world. Wesley calls it convincing proof that the patriarchs had a revelation of eternal glory; Clarke, evidence that they held the soul's immortality; Gill, that the desire spoken of is not theirs now in heaven but the desire they had on earth, common to all believers.
17:
Chrysostom marks what makes this trial different in kind. With Abel and Noah and Enoch there was an opposition of reasonings only; here what was of God seemed opposed to what was of God, faith against faith and command against promise. He had been told to leave his country for a land to be given him, and given no inheritance in it; he had been told that in Isaac his seed should be called, and was now commanded to offer Isaac.

Calvin calls it a singular instance of firmness, hardly matched anywhere: Abraham had proved what he was by many trials, but this surpassed every other, and the word used means no more than proved. Barnes traces that word through its other renderings, tempted and prove and examine and tried, and says it does not mean here, as it often does, the placing of inducements to lead a man wrong, but the testing of faith for genuineness and strength. Gill answers the moral objection: the command lays no ground for a charge of sin or cruelty against God, whose will is itself the rule of justice, who is Lord of life and may dispose of it as he thinks fit, and whose secret will was not that Isaac should die.

How far the sacrifice went they weigh in the tenses. Ellicott notes that the Greek says hath offered up, the reference being to the permanent record of Scripture, so that Abraham stands there as having offered his son. Robertson parses the participle of trial as present, the test still going on, and the verb of offering as perfect, the act consummated so far as Abraham was concerned when interrupted; the imperfect that follows is the tense of an interrupted action. Clarke fills in what was done: Abraham built an altar, bound his son, laid him on it and took the knife, and would have slain him had he not been stopped by the same authority that enjoined the sacrifice; Isaac is called only-begotten as the only son by his lawful wife, heir of his property and the promises. Wesley says the will was accepted as if he had done it.

Barnes points out that the promise excluded the bondwoman's son and ran through Isaac, implying he would reach manhood, and that Abraham believed this and yet deliberately prepared to put him to death. Gill and Ellicott both prefer to read the relative of Abraham, to whom it was said, as the Vulgate and Syriac render it. Robertson observes that God's own words were in Abraham's heart about his only son.

The solution stands in the same verse. Robertson puts it plainly: Abraham had God's clear command contravening God's own promise, and this was how he resolved it, since God who gave him Isaac in old age could raise him, and it was Abraham's duty to obey. Barnes reasons the same way and adds that no other way of fulfilling the promises remained. Gill is careful about the conclusion: his reasoning was the reasoning of faith, and concluded not that God would raise his son but that he was able to, Abraham having received him at first as from the dead. Ellicott takes the words as a general truth, that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Clarke infers that the resurrection must have been a doctrine of the patriarchs, since they expected a heavenly inheritance and saw that they died like other men. Wesley marks that no instance of it had yet occurred in the world. On the last phrase Calvin takes the word as likeness, Isaac not really rising but seeming in a manner to have risen when so suddenly rescued, and rejects Stuart's sense as far fetched; Clarke proposes that the word can mean a daring exploit, a jeoparding of the life; Robertson says only that Abraham received him back as almost from the dead.
20:
Calvin explains what makes a blessing an act of faith. To bless often means only to pray for a blessing, but Isaac's was an introduction into possession of the land God had promised, and yet he had nothing there but the right of burial, so that the titles he pronounced, that peoples should serve and tribes bow down, seemed strange from one hardly a free man. Barnes adds that no probabilities then existed on which such announcements could rest, so all Isaac said depended on his believing God had revealed it. Ellicott thinks the emphasis falls on the last words, since Isaac looked not to things near at hand but far into the future. Gill observes that the elder son, a wicked man, had a blessing too, since temporal blessings are enjoyed in common. Clarke cautions that the apostle does not intimate one to be an object of divine hatred and the other of divine love as to their eternal states, which is wholly a discovery of later ages. Chrysostom asks whether the righteous of old knew the things to come and answers most certainly, since if the Son was hidden from the weak he was with reason revealed to those conspicuous in virtue; though things to come may mean things future in this world.

The second instance draws them into a textual question. Barnes notes that the words quote the Greek version exactly, whereas the English of Genesis has Israel bowing on the bed's head, and explains that the same Hebrew consonants with different points mean a branch or rod or staff; the Masoretic points being of no authority, either translation is proper. Robertson adds that there is no word for leaning in the original at all. Ellicott reports that the Greek version and the Targums alike understood the act as worship, the translators taking the last Hebrew word for a staff. Clarke reconstructs the scene: Jacob was weak and confined to his couch, his staff at hand, either supporting his body or the ensign of his office as chief of a numerous family, since ancient chiefs kept such a staff beside them, as Homer shows. Wesley says he sat on the side of his bed. Ellicott adds that the verse gives its two events in reverse order of time, so that Jacob's blessing may follow immediately on the record before.

Calvin asks why Ephraim was preferred, and answers that the choice was not Jacob's: his eyes were dim with age, and he did not lay his right hand on the younger by chance but crossed his hands deliberately. Gill observes that the blessing came at the patriarchs' usual time for it, when a dying man's words would be the more attended to.

On the last instance the point is what wealth and honour failed to do. Gill says Joseph's riches, as they could not secure him from death, so they did not make him unmindful of it, nor proud, nor forgetful of his brethren's coming afflictions. Calvin presses further: honours did not make the holy man forget the promise nor detain him in Egypt, and in ordering his bones out he had no regard to himself, as though a grave in Canaan were sweeter, but meant only to sharpen his nation's desire for redemption. Barnes says the prediction could rest on nothing but faith. Robertson parses the participle as finishing his life and glosses the noun for the departing as a late compound for a way out. Ellicott traces the fulfilment to Moses carrying the bones out of Egypt and their burial at Shechem. Clarke ventures that the sarcophagus called Alexander's coffin is more probably Joseph's own, a conjecture the hieroglyphics may one day confirm. Henry draws the moral: things present are not the best things, and though faith serves through our whole lives it serves especially when we come to die.
23:
The faith at the birth is his parents', not Moses' own, as Gill and Barnes note, Barnes adding that Exodus names the mother because the concealment devolved on her. Calvin distinguishes their motive: heathens too have saved children at the peril of life from a mere desire of offspring, whereas these relied on the promise of a deliverer. He grants that the writer seems to say something contrary to faith in grounding the act on the child's beauty, and Ellicott resolves it, that the beauty was taken as a divine sign to guide their conduct; proper here carries its obsolete sense of handsome. Robertson traces the adjective to the word for a city, so that it means citified, of polished manners, occurring only here and in Stephen's speech. Wesley says they saw with a divine presage of things to come.

On the refusal the point pressed is its deliberateness. Barnes notes that Moses was then forty, taking the step in full maturity of judgment; Robertson says it in a phrase, that he was of age and chose not from ignorance. Gill glosses the expression as meaning he was great, a nobleman in Pharaoh's court. Clarke fills in what was surrendered: Moses was bred at the Egyptian court and likely to succeed to the throne, yet chose the lot of the oppressed people and God as his portion rather than pleasures which could only be temporary. Ellicott locates the act in the Greek of Exodus, where Moses first openly associates with his people: slaying the Egyptian who smote a Hebrew, he in act refused the name of Pharaoh's daughter's son. Calvin turns the example on the readers: of all instances this one the Jews ought most to have remembered, since through Moses they were delivered and the Law published; if faith is the main thing in Moses, all make poor proficiency in the Law who are not guided by it to faith.

What the choice cost stands in the comparisons. Gill says the people Moses joined were God's chosen and true worshippers, whose company is most eligible to every good man, and yet a poor and afflicted people. Barnes sets out both halves: crushed and despised, a nation of slaves, so joining them meant trial and delivering them peril. Ellicott prefers having chosen, as a deliberate act, and adds that to stand aloof for ease would have been apostasy, hence the alternative is called sin. Robertson parses the rare compound for being ill-treated along with others, and renders the other phrase as having temporary pleasure of sin.

The reproach of Christ divides them. Ellicott insists on the reproach of the Christ and rejects as impossible the renderings reproach for Christ and reproach like Christ's, since the words almost exactly quote a Messianic psalm where the enemies reproach the footsteps of the Anointed. Robertson agrees, applying the title to Jesus; there is today as then, he adds, a special reproach in following him. Clarke holds that the Messiah had been revealed to Moses, so the reproach God's people bore for opposing idolatry may be called by that name. Barnes offers three possibilities and inclines to a phrase understood then for sufferings borne in the cause of religion. Gill allows either Christ personal or Christ mystical, the church. Wesley takes it of what Moses bore for believing in the Messiah to come, and is exact about the recompense: not Canaan, which he never attained, but the future happiness his believing ancestors expected. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse to prove that it was Christ who appeared to Moses, setting it beside the saying that the rock was Christ, and concludes that the prophets then saw the Christ, as far as each was able. Calvin draws the practical rule, that we should shun as deadly poison whatever cannot be enjoyed without offending God, while the comforts a pure conscience allows are not included.
27:
Whether the forsaking is the flight to Midian or the Exodus splits them evenly. Barnes says most expositors take it of the departure with the people, evident from the added clause, since when Moses first fled it is expressly said he went because he feared. Clarke argues the same: at the flight he was in great fear, whereas before Pharaoh with God's authority he was without fear; Wesley agrees. Ellicott calls the question one of great difficulty and inclines the other way, reporting that the flight into Midian seems the view of all ancient writers and most moderns, on three grounds: the Passover is mentioned later, the second departure was at Pharaoh's request, and the verb is too personal for a national exodus. Gill takes it of the flight for the same reason of order; Calvin allows either and leans the same way. Robertson notes that the writer omits the slaying of the Egyptian.

On the Passover the interest is in what the act meant with the outcome hidden. Calvin says it was kept by faith not because the lamb was a type of Christ but because its benefit did not appear when the doorposts were sprinkled; it might well have seemed strange to set a few drops of blood against so great a destruction. Ellicott agrees, that the sprinkling was obedience with reference to a danger as yet unseen but present in God's word. Barnes presses the Greek, that the verb means more than celebrating and implies that Moses instituted the rite; Robertson takes the perfect as emphasising the feast's permanence. Chrysostom marvels at the compression: the writer includes manifold thought in brevity of expression, reminding them mid-exhortation of a type and mystery whereof they have the reality. Clarke reports an addition in one old Latin copy, that by faith they spoiled the Egyptians as they went out, and dismisses it as anything but genuine.

At the sea the same act divides two peoples. Clarke puts it sharply: the Egyptians thought they could walk through as well as the Israelites, tried, and were drowned, the one walking by faith and the other by sight. Calvin asks whence the difference came and answers that the Israelites had the word of God and the Egyptians had not, adding that many in that multitude were unbelieving and that the Lord granted to the faith of a few that the whole should pass. Barnes agrees that not all who passed can have had saving faith; Ellicott observes that the Egyptians made trial of the very thing in which Israel's faith consisted, but without the word to support them.

Of Jericho, Calvin says the city stood in their way at their first entrance, fortified and almost impregnable, and the command to walk round it appeared a work childish and ridiculous. Ellicott brings into relief the persistence of the obedience through seven days of almost total inaction, amid the contempt of their foes. Barnes says there was no natural tendency in the blowing of horns to produce the effect; Gill notes that Rahab's house stood on the wall and did not fall. On Rahab, Clarke argues that the words we translate harlot should rather be rendered innkeeper, there being no proper evidence for our version, and calls the notion of a later conversion a figment of an idle fancy; Gill supports this from the Targum, which calls her a woman that kept a victualling house, while Wesley says she was formerly one not of the fairest character. Calvin grants that the example may seem hardly entitled to notice for the meanness of the person. Ellicott prefers that they were disobedient to that they believed not, and observes that the same knowledge had come to her and to her countrymen, so that a despised heathen woman was united to the people of God while the men of Jericho perished.
32:
The turn in the chapter they all mark. Robertson parses the question as a deliberative subjunctive and a literary and oratorical idiom, the writer helpless to continue in the style kept from Abel to Rahab; the second clause he renders as will leave me telling about, and notes that the masculine participle disposes of Priscilla as author. Clarke says the expression is usual with the best Greek writers when much remains but must be omitted. Henry calls it the preface of a divine orator, introducing a summary in which the acts are not ascribed to particular persons but left to be applied by those acquainted with the sacred story. Calvin explains the change: it was to be feared that by naming a few the writer should seem to confine the praise of faith to a few, and there would be no end if he dwelt on every instance, what he said of a few extending to the whole Church of God. Ellicott observes that enough has been said to guide all willing to search the Scriptures; Gill, that the writer had said enough and yet not all he could.

Calvin dwells on how unpromising the chosen men were. It seemed strange to attack an immense host with three hundred, and the shaking of pitchers appeared a sham alarm; the next was inferior to his enemies and guided only by a woman's counsel; another was a countryman who had never borne arms. Clarke gives the outcomes: a countless multitude of Midianites destroyed, Jabin overthrown, the Philistine yoke broken. Barnes adds that Barak's yielding to the prophetess, who summoned him in the Lord's name, was itself evidence of confidence. Wesley notes that after Samuel the prophets are properly mentioned, David being a prophet too, though a king.

Robertson counts what follows as nine terse clauses, in Moffatt's phrase, set down without a connective, and finds great force in the sledge-hammer style. Ellicott prefers overcame kingdoms and applies the words to all the deliverers named. On the promises he raises a genuine question: do the words mean these men won promises of future blessing, or that promises of deliverance were fulfilled to them? He sees no reason to doubt that both are included. Barnes takes them as promised blessings, with Bloomfield and Stuart. Clarke supposes a reference to Joshua and Caleb, who obtained the land while the rest were excluded, to Phinehas, who received an everlasting priesthood, and to David, who obtained the kingdom. Gill lists David's conquests and concludes that war is in some cases lawful and that believers need not fear kings. Wesley distributes the clauses among the men, and observes that the more ancient examples are subjoined in an inverted order.

On the fire and the sword the older instances are agreed. Barnes and Clarke both name the three Hebrews in the furnace, and both take the recovery out of weakness of Hezekiah. Robertson renders the second clause as the mouths of the sword and glosses the last noun as an encampment, and so armies drawn up in battle line. Calvin reports an older reading referring the raising up from weakness to the restoration of the Jews from exile, when they were like men without hope, allows the application to Hezekiah, and would extend it to every raising up of the saints when cast down. Ellicott alone looks forward rather than back: though these clauses trace easily to the heroes of the Old Testament, the writer's thought seems to rest mainly on the Maccabean times, since the next verse is acknowledged to draw on the second book and no words could more truly characterise the contents of the first. Gill turns each clause into a spiritual application: believers are delivered out of the fire of affliction and shall not be hurt of the second death. Wesley closes in a sentence: faith animates to the most heroic enterprises, civil and military.
35:
Ellicott marks the hinge: here the record changes, from the victories of faith in action to its triumph over suffering, so that those who escaped the sword and those slain with it alike exemplify one power. Wesley says the same, that from those who acted great things the apostle rises higher, to those who showed faith by suffering. Calvin insists the two kinds are one at bottom: at first view they widely differ, since some triumphed over vanquished enemies and were rescued from the midst of death, while others were shamefully treated, consumed by want and so hated that they had to hide themselves; yet all persevered invincible even to death.

The word for the first torment they cannot settle. Barnes derives it from the drum and describes a torture named from the instrument. Clarke says the critics are not agreed, the root signifying a baton used in bastinadoing criminals, and inclines to the bastinado on the soles of the feet. Robertson takes it as a late verb meaning to beat the drum and so to beat to death. Ellicott supplies the case that fits, the aged Eleazar martyred for refusing swine's flesh. Robertson notes that the deliverance refused was offered at the price of disloyalty, Wesley that it was refused on sinful terms; the better resurrection Wesley explains as a higher reward, the greater their sufferings the greater their glory.

Of the mockings Clarke says they can never mean Ishmael's against Isaac or the taunts of the youths of Bethel, and thinks it likelier that public exhibitions of God's people at idol feasts are meant, Samson before Dagon being quite in point. Barnes observes that scourging usually preceded a martyr's death. Ellicott calls the bonds a lasting and cruel captivity, worse even than mockings. Gill names Naboth and the Zechariah slain in the court of the Lord's house, and recalls that Jerusalem's character is that she stoned the prophets sent to her. On the sawing asunder all who mention it report the tradition about Isaiah, Clarke citing the Talmudic account that Manasseh commanded him slain with a wooden saw, and Robertson calling it a cruel Jewish punishment.

The next word puzzles them. Ellicott calls it very remarkable in such a position and reports many conjectures resting on a supposed scribal error, but holds that if the text stands the writer means the promises and allurements used against the persecuted. Robertson agrees that the manuscripts vary greatly, and calls the mild word an anticlimax after the sawing. Wesley resolves it by the arrangement, that torments and enticements are named alternately, so that they were tried every way, by threatenings and tortures and again by promises.

On the parenthesis they are unanimous and warm. Calvin observes that as the prophets wandered among wild beasts they might have seemed unworthy to be sustained on the earth, since they found no place among men, but that the apostle inverts the sentiment; wherever God's servants come they bring his blessing like a sweet odour, as Potiphar's house was blessed for Joseph and Sodom would have been spared for ten righteous men. Barnes calls it a most beautiful expression, at once a statement of their holiness and of the wickedness of the rest of mankind. Gill explains why it stands in a parenthesis, to prevent the objection that they were restless persons who made disturbance and were deservedly punished. Robertson calls it a graphic picture in a short relative clause, and describes the wanderers as lost sheep hunted by wolves. Clarke recalls Elijah and the hundred prophets hidden in caves by Obadiah. Chrysostom draws it home: whenever he reflects on the achievements of the saints, despondency about his own condition comes over him, since we have not even in dreams experienced the things among which those men spent their lives, not paying the penalty of sins but always doing rightly and yet always afflicted.
39:
Ellicott notes that with the history concluded the word used at the head of the chapter is resumed, and sets beside this verse two others: that Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise, and that the readers need endurance to receive it. To the saints of the Old Testament the blessing was future: obtained, but not within this present life. Robertson adds that individual promises were fulfilled to them but the Messianic promise they did not live to see. Barnes says they did not receive the fulfilment, or not all that was promised. Clarke states what was missing: they heard of the promises made to Abraham of a heavenly rest and of the Messiah, for this was a constant tradition, but died without seeing this Anointed of the Lord. Wesley calls it the heavenly inheritance. Gill allows the phrase to be limited to the sufferers just described, whom the Ethiopic version calls witnesses concerning the faith, or extended to all the chapter's instances.

Calvin reads the conclusion as an argument from the less to the greater. If they on whom the light of grace had not yet so brightly shone displayed so great a constancy in enduring evils, what ought the full brightness of the Gospel to produce in us? A small spark led them to heaven; now that the sun of righteousness shines over us, what pretence excuses us if we still cleave to the earth? Henry draws the same inference: since God provided better things for these readers, they might be sure he expected as good things from them, and as our advantages exceed theirs, so should our obedience and love be greater; unless we get true faith such as these believers had, they will rise up to condemn us at the last day. He adds that the world thinks the righteous unworthy to live in it while God declares the world unworthy of them.

What the better thing is they answer variously. Gill excludes the obvious candidates: not a church free from persecution, which is the lot of saints under both Testaments, nor the felicity of the soul after death, nor any greater happiness hereafter, all common to believers of every age; but Christ himself, now exhibited in the flesh. The difference is only this, that they had Christ in the promise and we have him that was promised, they in type and shadow and we in reality. Clarke makes it the Gospel dispensation with its privileges; Ellicott prefers the preposition concerning us, and defines the better thing as better than they had received. Robertson parses the genitive absolute of a late compound meaning to foresee, identifies the thing as the better promises named earlier, and warns that this reflects no merit in us but the fulness of the time in God's dispensation of grace. Wesley names it everlasting glory.

On the last clause they converge. Clarke holds that believers before the flood, after it, under the law and since make but one Church, which cannot be reckoned complete till believers under all dispensations are gathered, so that the earlier cannot be consummated even in glory until the Gospel Church arrives in the heaven of heavens; he supports it from the white robes given to those told to rest a little season. Barnes reasons from the system rather than the persons: revelation was not complete in one generation but required successive ages, so that our existence and the developments of our own times were as necessary to its perfection as the promise made to the patriarchs. Ellicott states the design directly, that they and we may be perfected together, first in the joint reception of mature knowledge through the high-priestly work of Christ, and then that we with them may at the end have our consummation and bliss in body and soul. Wesley says it in a phrase: that we might all be perfected together in heaven.
